title: Your Urge to Breathe Isn't About Oxygen
topic: What happens to your body when you hold your breath?

beats.label: hold your breath
lines: Your urge to breathe mostly isn't about oxygen.

beats.title: While you hold it
lines: Hold your breath, and your oxygen stores start running down.
But the urge to breathe is driven mainly by rising carbon dioxide, not falling oxygen.
That's why fast, deep breathing before a dive is so dangerous.
It lowers carbon dioxide, delays the warning, and can fool your brain into feeling comfortable while oxygen sinks.

beats.title: The trip up
lines: The riskiest moment is the way up. As a diver rises, oxygen pressure in the lungs drops, and oxygen can fall so fast that blackout comes within seconds.
And the victims are often fit, strong swimmers who have done many dives before.
So if a breath hold feels easy, don't trust it: stay within your limits and come up slowly.

sources.claim: Breath-hold duration is limited by oxygen reserves and the response to raised carbon dioxide; the urge to breathe is primarily driven by rising carbon dioxide rather than falling oxygen.
Hyperventilation before a dive reduces carbon dioxide, delays the body's warning signals and can mislead the brain into feeling comfortable as oxygen drops to dangerous levels.
Blackouts are more likely on ascent, when partial pressure in the lungs drops and oxygen can fall so blackout occurs within seconds; victims are often fit, strong, experienced divers.
Safety guidelines advise divers to keep within their limits, be aware of their body signals, and ascend slowly.
